actions.scriptText:
Plain Kefir!
-
Ranked!
-
1 gram of fat. Saturated fat is only 0.66 grams and cholesterol is just 5 milligrams, so there is not much fat baggage here. Polyunsaturated fat is only 0.05 grams though, meaning kefir is not bringing much useful unsaturated fat either. For dairy, keeping the saturated fat and cholesterol down is a useful win.
-
4.8 grams of carbs. Most of that comes from lactose, the natural sugar found in milk. The glycemic index is around 30, so it should behave fairly steadily compared with sugary drinks. Fibre is 0 grams, which is completely normal for dairy but means your fruit, grains, or vegetables still need to handle digestion support. For dairy, carbs are mostly a sugar check.
-
3.8 grams of protein. That gives the drink some substance, but it is not enough to make kefir a serious protein food on its own. It can help at breakfast or in a smoothie, but something like Greek yogurt brings much more protein in the same amount. For dairy, protein matters, and kefir is more of a supporter than main character.
-
Vitamin A is 19% daily value, a useful amount for vision, skin, and immune support. Vitamin B12 is 12% daily value, helping nerves and red blood-cell production. Vitamin D is only 5% daily value, so it adds a little bone and immune support but is not doing much heavy lifting. For dairy, this is a decent little vitamin mix rather than a standout one.
-
Calcium is 10% daily value, giving some useful bone and tooth support. Magnesium and potassium are both around 3% daily value, so they barely help with muscle function, fluid balance, or the wider mineral picture. For dairy, calcium is the main mineral job, and kefir does that reasonably well, but without offering much else.
-
The upsides first: traditional kefir grains are tiny microbe communities. They are reusable clusters of bacteria and yeast, not cereal grains, which is honestly a pretty strange little food fact. Fermentation can make lactose easier to handle. A small human study found plain kefir was better tolerated than milk by adults who struggle to digest lactose. The drinkable format is genuinely handy. Have it straight from the fridge, blend it into a smoothie, or use it as a tangy base for dressings.
-
The drawbacks next: sweetened bottles can change the whole deal. Added sugar can turn a useful fermented drink into something much closer to a liquid dessert. Milk allergy is still a hard stop. Fermentation can change the lactose, but it does not remove the milk proteins that trigger an allergy. The sour, slightly funky flavour is not for everyone. Plain kefir tastes much tangier than ordinary milk or sweetened yogurt.
-
Best bits are the light fat profile, useful vitamin A, some calcium, and the genuinely interesting fermentation story. Weak spots are modest protein, no fibre, low magnesium and potassium, and how quickly sweetened versions can lose the plot. Best for an easy fermented breakfast drink, smoothies, or adding some dairy variety without loads of saturated fat. Keep it plain and let fruit handle the sweetness.
-
C tier.

Fermentation can make lactose easier to handle. A small human study found plain kefir was better tolerated than milk by adults who struggle to digest lactose. The drinkable format is genuinely handy. Have it straight from the fridge, blend it into a smoothie, or use it as a tangy base for dressings.
-
The drawbacks next: sweetened bottles can change the whole deal. Added sugar can turn a useful fermented drink into something much closer to a liquid dessert. Milk allergy is still a hard stop. Fermentation can change the lactose, but it does not remove the milk proteins that trigger an allergy. The sour, slightly funky flavour is not for everyone. Plain kefir tastes much tangier than ordinary milk or sweetened yogurt.
-
Best bits are the light fat profile, useful vitamin A, some calcium, and the genuinely interesting fermentation story. Weak spots are modest protein, no fibre, low magnesium and potassium, and how quickly sweetened versions can lose the plot. Best for an easy fermented breakfast drink, smoothies, or adding some dairy variety without loads of saturated fat. Keep it plain and let fruit handle the sweetness.

actions.scriptText:
Cannellini Beans!
-
Ranked!
-
2.2 grams of fat. Saturated fat is only 0.22 grams, an excellent low mark. Polyunsaturated fat is just 0.36 grams, so the beans do not provide much useful fat either. That is not a major problem though. Legumes are supposed to win through slow carbs, fibre, and protein, not fat.
-
59.8 grams of carbs. Starch is 29.9 grams, providing useful staple energy. Fibre is an excellent 15.2 grams, supporting digestion and helping slow the carb response. The glycemic index is only 31, meaning the carbs raise blood glucose relatively slowly. For legumes, this combination of fibre and low glycemic behaviour is one of the main wins.
-
21.6 grams of protein. Essential amino acids score 9 out of 9, meaning all 9 groups the body must obtain from food clear the useful threshold. Bioavailability is 80%, a solid result for bean protein. For legumes, useful protein combined with slow carbs is the whole point, and cannellini beans deliver both.
-
Vitamins barely show up here. Vitamin E is only 1% daily value and vitamin C is 0%. Vitamin C helps the body absorb plant-based iron, so pairing cannellini beans with peppers, lemon, or other vitamin C-rich foods makes nutritional sense. On their own though, the vitamin section is a clear weakness.
-
Iron and magnesium are both 37% daily value. Iron supports haemoglobin and oxygen transport, while magnesium supports energy production plus normal nerve and muscle function. Zinc is the softer mark at 25% daily value, but that is still useful for immune function and tissue repair. For legumes, this is a genuinely strong mineral section.
-
The positives first: creamy texture works in proper meals. They blend into soups and sauces while still holding their shape in salads. Cheap dry pantry staple. A bag stores well and turns into several meals for very little money. Mild flavour takes seasoning well. Herbs, tomato, garlic, and stronger sauces all work.
-
The cons next: can be rough on digestion. Their fermentable carbohydrates feed gut bacteria, but can also produce gas and bloating. Dry beans take time and planning. Soaking and a full cook make them less convenient than opening a can. They must be cooked properly. Cannellini are white kidney beans, and raw or undercooked beans can retain a natural lectin called P H A. Proper cooking brings it down to safe levels.
-
Best bits are fibre, a low glycemic index, strong plant protein, and excellent minerals. Weak spots are thin vitamin support, possible digestive discomfort, and dry-bean preparation. Best for steady energy, digestion, and budget meals because fibre supports bowel health, while protein and starch make them a substantial staple. Pair them with vitamin C-rich vegetables to improve iron absorption.
-
B tier.

actions.scriptText:
Beef Sirloin!
-
Ranked!
-
12.7 grams of fat. Cholesterol is 75 milligrams, which is a fairly controlled mark for a meat. Polyunsaturated fat is only 0.48 grams, so very little of the fat comes from that more heart-friendly type. Saturated fat is 5.2 grams, which adds some real baggage. For meats, the fat mix decides how much baggage comes with the protein.
-
0 grams of carbs. There is no sugar, starch, or fibre to score, which is completely normal for plain beef. That makes sirloin easy to fit into a lower-carb meal, but your vegetables or sides still need to bring the fibre. For meats, carbs are not the job unless something is added.
-
20.4 grams of protein. Essential amino acids score 9 out of 9. That means all nine amino acids your body cannot make on its own show up in useful amounts, helping muscle repair and maintenance. Collagen is only 1.6 grams, so sirloin is not doing much on that structural-protein side. For meats, usable complete protein is the main job, and sirloin nails that part.
-
Vitamin B12 is 44% daily value. B12 helps your nerves work properly and helps make red blood cells, which carry oxygen around the body. The rest of the vitamin panel is very quiet. For meats, B12 is a real strength, but one strong vitamin does not equal broad vitamin coverage.
-
Zinc is 32% daily value, a strong amount for immune function and wound healing. Potassium is only 7% daily value, so it does not bring much help with fluid balance or normal muscle function. Iron is 9% daily value, useful but smaller than beef's reputation might suggest. For meats, zinc and iron can add value beyond protein, and zinc does most of that work here.
-
The upsides first: a plain whole cut keeps processing low. There is no curing, breading, or long ingredient list getting in the way. Easy to build a proper meal around. Add vegetables and a carb and dinner is basically sorted. Works across plenty of simple meals. Grill it, pan-sear it, slice it into wraps, or throw it into a stir-fry.
-
The drawbacks next: the fat trim can change the numbers fast. A leaner piece and a heavily marbled piece are not the same food in practice. Overcooking can make it dry and tough. Sirloin rewards a little attention in the pan. Cost and cold storage add some friction. It is pricier and less convenient than a shelf-stable meal anchor.
-
Best bits are complete, highly usable protein, vitamin B12, zinc, and being an easy whole-cut meal anchor. Weak spots are the middling fat profile, low potassium, thin vitamin range, and how much the trim changes the result. Best for muscle-focused meals and practical dinners because it gives you serious protein without processed-meat baggage. Pair it with vegetables and a fibre-rich carb, and keep an eye on the fat trim.
-
B tier.

actions.scriptText:
Farro!
-
Ranked!
-
3.1 grams of fat. Saturated fat is only 0.5 grams, a strong mark that keeps the fat profile light. Omega 3 is 100 milligrams, far too little to make farro a useful omega 3 source. Fat is not a grain's main job, but this section is clean rather than powerful.
-
72.1 grams of carbs. Starch is 61.7 grams, providing the grain's main source of energy. Sugar is 0 grams, but the glycemic index is still 63, which is only moderate. This is a good lesson: low sugar does not automatically mean low glycemic, because starch also becomes glucose. For grains, carb behaviour matters more than carb amount.
-
12.6 grams of protein. Essential amino acids score 8 out of 9, so most of the amino acid groups your body must get from food clear the useful threshold. Nonessential amino acids score 8 out of 11, but these matter less because the body can make them. Bioavailability is 80%, a solid result for grain protein. For grains, this is valuable extra support, although carbs remain the main role.
-
Vitamins are low across the board. Vitamin E is the best mark at only 5% daily value. Vitamin E helps protect cells from oxidative damage, but this amount is too small to make farro a meaningful source. For grains, that leaves the energy, protein, and mineral sections doing the work.
-
Zinc is 36% daily value, a strong amount for immune function and tissue repair. Calcium is only 2% daily value, so farro contributes very little towards bone mineral needs. Minerals can make a grain more than just starch, and zinc manages that here.
-
The upsides first: chewy texture holds up in full meals. It stays distinct in soups, salads, and grain bowls instead of turning to mush. Batch-cooks into a practical meal base. One pot can cover several meals and carry stronger toppings. Pearled farro is easier to cook. Removing some outer bran shortens the cooking time and makes the grain more approachable.
-
The drawbacks next: pearling strips away part of the bran. Bran is the fibre and micronutrient-rich outer layer, so easier cooking comes with a nutrition tradeoff. Contains gluten. Because farro is wheat, it is unsuitable for coeliac disease and gluten-free diets. Still needs cooking and planning. It is less instant than rice or couscous and definitely is not grab-and-go.
-
Best bits are strong grain protein, a clean fat profile, useful zinc, and a practical chewy meal role. Weak spots are the moderate glycemic index, very low vitamins and calcium, plus some nutrition lost through pearling. Best for energy and practical meals: the starch fuels activity, while the protein and sturdy texture make it a useful base for bowls, soups, and salads. This is a solid grain, but it still needs other foods around it for a rounded meal.
-
B tier.

actions.scriptText:
Pistachios (Roasted & Salted)!
-
Ranked!
-
45.8 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 5.6 grams, a strong mark relative to the total fat. Omega 3 is only 212 milligrams, so this is not an omega 3-rich nut. For nuts, fat quality has to justify the calorie density. This is a mixed section: a clean saturated-fat mark, but weak omega 3.
-
27.6 grams of carbs. Fibre is 10.3 grams, helping digestion and slowing the absorption of the other carbs. Starch is only 1.4 grams, but nuts are not supposed to be starch-based energy foods. The glycemic index is 30, meaning these carbs raise blood glucose relatively slowly. For nuts, fibre and glycemic behaviour matter far more than starch.

blocks.text: Salmon!
Ranked!

13 grams of fat. Omega 3 is 2200 milligrams, which is a huge strength here. Saturated fat is 3.1 grams, so the fat profile stays pretty clean for a meat. For meats, fat quality is the main tradeoff, and salmon handles that really well.
No defensible carb submacros to call out. For meats, carbs barely matter unless something has been added, so this section is basically neutral.

20.4 grams of protein. Essential amino acids score is 9 out of 9, and nonessential amino acids score is 10 out of 11, so the protein quality is strong. Collagen is only 0.3 grams, so the structural-protein side is weak. For meats, complete protein matters a lot, and the 94% bioavailability does bring it back up a lot too.

Vitamin B12 is 117% daily value, which is excellent for nerve and blood-cell support. Vitamin D is 66% daily value, which is also a serious mark for bone and immune support. Vitamin C is 0, but for meats, B12 and vitamin D matter much more.

Minerals are the weak section. Potassium is 8% daily value, which is the best number here but still low. Iron is only 4% daily value, and zinc is only 4% too. For meats, minerals can add value, but salmon is not winning through this section.

The upsides first: easy to build a strong meal around. Works as a real centrepiece food. Helps meals feel complete. Very useful when you want protein without needing lots of extras. Strong healthy-food reputation. In this case, the reputation actually matches the numbers.

Cons next: can be expensive. Price can make it less practical. Quality varies with sourcing. Wild, farmed, fresh, and frozen versions can shift the real-world result. Needs good storage and handling. It is not as easy as shelf-stable protein.

Best bits are omega 3, vitamin B12, vitamin D, and complete protein. Weak spots are the low minerals, and the practical issues around price, sourcing, and storage. Best as a protein-and-fat source for heart health, muscle support, bone support, immune support, and practical high-protein meals.
S tier.

blocks.text: Rice Cakes!
Ranked!

3 grams of fat. Saturated fat is only 0.6 grams, so the fat profile is pretty clean. Omega 3 is just 20 milligrams, though, so there is basically no seed-style fat upside here. For grains, fat is generally all around low anyway.

81.5 grams of carbs. Starch is 77 grams, so rice cakes do bring quick staple-carb energy. But the glycemic index is 82, which is rough for steadier carb behaviour, and 4.3 grams of fibre is not enough to rescue it. Carb quality matters most for grains.

7 grams of protein. The essential amino acids score is 0 out of 9, and the nonessential amino acids score is 0 out of 11, so this is not doing much as a protein food, but this is to be expected. For grains, protein can help, but rice cakes are mostly just puffed carb.

Vitamins are low overall. Vitamin E is only 1% daily value, and there is no meaningful vitamin backup here. For grains, that is not automatically fatal, but rice cakes do not make up for it elsewhere.

Magnesium is 13% daily value, which is the best mineral mark, but still a little low. Calcium is only 2% daily value, and iron and zinc stay low too. For grains, minerals can help round out the score, but this section is weak.

D tier.

episode.narrationText:
Fennel Seeds!
-
Ranked!
-
15 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 0.5 grams, which is nice and low. Omega 3 is 250 milligrams, helping a bit, but not enough to be amazing for seeds. Polyunsaturated fat is 6 grams, which sounds solid, but for seeds it is still not doing loads. There is 9.9 grams of monounsaturated fats though, which brings the score back up a bit.
-
52 grams of carbs. Fibre is 40 grams, which is massive and easily the best part here. Glycemic index is 15, helping with steadier carb behaviour. Starch is 10 grams, adding some usable carb energy, but fibre is clearly doing the heavy lifting. For seeds, carbs matter most when fibre is this strong.
-
16 grams of protein. That is decent on paper, but it still is not really carrying the food. Essential amino acids score is 0 out of 9, not giving much repair-and-maintenance protein support. For seeds, protein helps, but it needs better quality to become the main reason to use them.
-
Vitamins are not really showing up here. Vitamin E is 7% daily value, which is too low to score. For seeds, vitamin E matters most, and fennel seeds are not bringing enough of it.
-
Calcium is 120% daily value, which is huge for bone support. Iron is 100% daily value, adding real oxygen-transport support. Magnesium is 96% daily value, also helping with muscle and nerve support. For seeds, minerals are the clearest reason this works on the stat sheet.
-
The upsides first: tiny food with real nutrient density. The numbers are genuinely serious for something this small. Easy to add into meals. A small amount can fit into cooking without changing the whole plate. Richer texture can help satisfaction. That can make a sprinkle feel more useful than plain seasoning.
-
The drawbacks next: spice-like portions cap the real payoff. The numbers are huge, but the real serving is tiny. Strong flavour can take over a dish. That anise-like taste is useful, but it is not exactly neutral. Whole seeds can be awkward to eat. Texture and chewing matter, especially when they are sprinkled in rather than ground.
-
Best bits are fibre, calcium, iron, and magnesium. Weak spots are low vitamin E, limited protein quality, and the fact that normal portions are tiny. Best as a small mineral-and-fibre boost in cooking, not as a main food. Basically, the score sheet looks strong, but real-life serving sizes pull it back down.
-
C tier.

narrationBlocks.text: Tater Tots!
Ranked!

9.6 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 2.2 grams, which is a little heavy for a tuber food. Polyunsaturated fat is 2.8 grams, helping a little with useful unsaturated fat. Fat isn't the main job for tubers though.

24 grams of carbs. Starch is 16 grams, giving some steady carb energy. However, the glycemic index is 74, which is really not the best for steady carb behaviour, and this does hurt the score for tubers. Sugar is 0.5 grams but that is to be expected from tubers. For tubers, carb quality decides a lot.
2.3 grams of protein. Protein barely matters here. And that's all that really needs to be said about this section. The focus of tubers lies in other sections.
Vitamins are not really showing up here. For tubers, vitamins can lift up a staple carb, but these are definitely not doing that.
Potassium is 8% daily value, the best number here but still too low to carry this section. For tubers, minerals matter most when potassium shows up strongly.

The upsides first: easy freezer-side convenience. That makes them simple and convenient. Crisp texture can feel satisfying. That helps explain the snack appeal. The drawbacks next: still a processed fried snack. The original potato identity is not enough to save it. Cooking methods and preparation can impact a lot. Deep frying can push calories up to around 250 and add about 7 grams of fat. Easy to overeat as a side. Small pieces make casual portions creep up quickly.

episode.narrationText:
Tater Tots!
-
Ranked!
-
9.6 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 2.2 grams, which is a little heavy for a tuber food. Polyunsaturated fat is 2.8 grams, helping a little with useful unsaturated fat. Fat isn't the main job for tubers though.
-
24 grams of carbs. Starch is 16 grams, giving some steady carb energy. However, the glycemic index is 74, which is really not the best for steady carb behaviour, and this does hurt the score for tubers. Sugar is 0.5 grams but that is to be expected from tubers. For tubers, carb quality decides a lot.
-
2.3 grams of protein. Protein barely matters here. And that's all that really needs to be said about this section. The focus of tubers lies in other sections.
-
Vitamins are not really showing up here. For tubers, vitamins can lift up a staple carb, but these are definitely not doing that.
-
Potassium is 8% daily value, the best number here but still too low to carry this section. For tubers, minerals matter most when potassium shows up strongly.
-
The upsides first: easy freezer-side convenience. That makes them simple and convenient. Crisp texture can feel satisfying. That helps explain the snack appeal. Homemade versions can improve the health score a lot. Ingredients used matter of course, but not as much as simply leaving out all the additives used in prepackaged versions.
-
The drawbacks next: still a processed fried snack. The original potato identity is not enough to save it. Cooking methods and preparation can impact a lot. Deep frying can push calories up to around 250 and add about 7 grams of fat. Easy to overeat as a side. Small pieces make casual portions creep up quickly.
-
Best bits are convenience, texture, and some starch energy. Weak spots are glycemic index, low potassium, and the processed fried format. Best for occasional comfort-food sides, not daily staple carbs. Essentially this convenience food format takes a basic tuber idea and just makes the nutrition tradeoff worse.
-
Slop tier.

episode.narrationText:
Tater Tots!
-
Ranked!
-
9.6 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 2.2 grams, which is a little heavy for a tuber food. Polyunsaturated fat is 2.8 grams, helping a little with useful unsaturated fat. Fat isn't the main job for tubers though.
-
24 grams of carbs. Starch is 16 grams, giving some steady carb energy. However, the glycemic index is 74, which is really not the best for steady carb behaviour, and this does hurt the score for tubers. Sugar is 0.5 grams but that is to be expected from tubers. For tubers, carb quality decides a lot.
-
2.3 grams of protein. Protein barely matters here. And that's all that really needs to be said about this section. The focus of tubers lies in other sections.
-
Vitamins are not really showing up here. For tubers, vitamins can lift up a staple carb, but these are definitely not doing that.
-
Potassium is 8% daily value, the best number here but still too low to carry this section. For tubers, minerals matter most when potassium shows up strongly.
-
The upsides first: easy freezer-side convenience. That makes them simple and convenient. Crisp texture can feel satisfying. That helps explain the snack appeal. Homemade versions can improve the health score a lot. Ingredients used matter of course, but not as much as simply leaving out all the additives used in prepackaged versions.
-
The drawbacks next: still a processed fried snack. The original potato identity is not enough to save it. Cooking methods and preparation can impact a lot. Deep frying can push calories up to around 250 and add about 7 grams of fat. Easy to overeat as a side. Small pieces make casual portions creep up quickly.
-
Best bits are convenience, texture, and some starch energy. Weak spots are glycemic index, low potassium, and the processed fried format. Best for occasional comfort-food sides, not daily staple carbs. Essentially this convenience food format takes a basic tuber idea and just makes the nutrition tradeoff worse.
-
Slop tier.

blocks.text: Cranberries!
Ranked!
0.1 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 0.01 grams, supporting a cleaner fat profile. Although the fat profile is almost irrelevant for fruits.

12.0 grams of carbs. Glycemic index is low at 45, meaning the carbs should land slower and steadier. Fibre is 3.6 grams, which gives a better fullness and digestion signal than most light fruits. Sugar is 4.3 grams, which is low for fruit and helps the carb section. Sugar control and fibre are the most important parts of the carbohydrate profile of fruits.
0.5 grams of protein. Not enough protein to be a real strength. For fruits, protein isn't really something to rely on.

Vitamin C is 16% daily value, useful for collagen formation and antioxidant support. Vitamin A is basically 0% daily value, not bringing much vision or immune support. For fruit, vitamin C and vitamin A matter most.

Potassium is 2% daily value, which is the best tracked mineral here, but still too low to matter much. Iron is only 1% daily value, not bringing much oxygen-transport support. For fruit, minerals are mostly just an extra bonus, and only matter when they are in amounts that actually mean something.

Pros first: sharp tart flavour tool. A small amount can brighten sauces, oats, salads, or baking without needing much fruit volume. Freezes well. It holds up well from frozen, so it is easier to keep around than many soft fresh fruits. Polyphenol-rich skin. The deep red skin brings a stronger plant-compound angle than many mild fruits.

Cons next: too tart for plain snacking. Most people do not eat raw cranberries by the handful, so the practical snack role is limited. Often needs added sugar. Cranberry sauces, juices, and dried versions commonly rely on sweetening to make the flavour work. Seasonal and recipe-dependent. Fresh cranberries are not as effortless year-round as everyday fruits like apples, bananas, or berries.
Best bits are low glycemic index and fibre. Weak spots are low minerals and vitamin A. Best for sharp low-calorie flavour swaps, and it makes a nice sauce. But that's about it.
D tier.

narrationBlocks.text: Cranberries!
Ranked!
0.1 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 0.01 grams, supporting a cleaner fat profile. Although the fat profile is almost irrelevant for fruits.

12.0 grams of carbs. Glycemic index is low at 45, meaning the carbs should land slower and steadier. Fibre is 3.6 grams, which gives a better fullness and digestion signal than most light fruits. Sugar is 4.3 grams, which is low for fruit and helps the carb section. Sugar control and fibre are the most important parts of the carbohydrate profile of fruits.
0.5 grams of protein. Not enough protein to be a real strength. For fruits, protein isn't really something to rely on.

Vitamin C is 16% daily value, useful for collagen formation and antioxidant support. Vitamin A is basically 0% daily value, not bringing much vision or immune support. For fruit, vitamin C and vitamin A matter most.

Potassium is 2% daily value, which is the best tracked mineral here, but still too low to matter much. Iron is only 1% daily value, not bringing much oxygen-transport support. For fruit, minerals are mostly just an extra bonus, and only matter when they are in amounts that actually mean something.

Pros first: sharp tart flavour tool. A small amount can brighten sauces, oats, salads, or baking without needing much fruit volume. Freezes well. It holds up well from frozen, so it is easier to keep around than many soft fresh fruits. Polyphenol-rich skin. The deep red skin brings a stronger plant-compound angle than many mild fruits.

Cons next: too tart for plain snacking. Most people do not eat raw cranberries by the handful, so the practical snack role is limited. Often needs added sugar. Cranberry sauces, juices, and dried versions commonly rely on sweetening to make the flavour work. Seasonal and recipe-dependent. Fresh cranberries are not as effortless year-round as everyday fruits like apples, bananas, or berries.
Best bits are low glycemic index and fibre. Weak spots are low minerals and vitamin A. Best for sharp low-calorie flavour swaps, and it makes a nice sauce. But that's about it.

episode.narrationText:
Plums!
-
Ranked!
-
0.3 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 0.017 grams, supporting a cleaner fat profile. Although the fat profile isn't that important for fruits.
-
11.4 grams of carbs. Glycemic index is low at 39, meaning carbs release slower and steadier, this helps avoid sharp blood sugar spikes. Fibre is 1.4 grams, which provides only a modest fullness and digestion support, this matters as fiber is an important factor for fruits. Sugar control and fibre are the most important bits of the carbohydrate profile of fruits.
-
0.7 grams of protein. Not enough protein to be a real strength. For fruits, protein isn't really something to look out for.
-
Vitamin C is 11% daily value, useful for collagen formation and antioxidant support. Vitamin A is only 2% daily value, not bringing much vision or immune support. For fruit, vitamin C and vitamin A matter most.
-
Potassium is 3% daily value, which may be the best number here, but still too low to matter much. All other minerals aren't worth talking about. For fruit, minerals are mostly just an extra bonus, and only matter when they are actually worth talking about.
-
Pros first: easy fresh-fruit snack. It works with no peeling or cooking, so it is easy to use when the fruit is ripe. Peel adds tart colour. Keeping the skin gives more plum colour, texture, and sharp-sweet contrast. Works fresh or cooked. It can go into yoghurt, oats, salads, compote, sauces, or desserts without much effort.
-
Cons next: bruises easily. Soft fruit bruises quickly, so quality can drop fast after transport or storage. Ripeness window is short. The best eating window is narrow, and underripe or overripe plums are much less useful. Stone interrupts snacking. The pit makes them less convenient than fully edible bite-size fruit like berries or grapes.
-
Best bits are that it's an easy fresh-fruit snack and low glycemic index. Weak spots are low fiber and low vitamin A. Best for quick on the go snacks, low-calorie to volume ratio, and its ability to compliment many other foods.
-
D tier.
